item.title: Why Certain Pop Songs Trigger Inexplicable Emotion
item.description:
Neuroscience

Why Certain Pop Songs Trigger Inexplicable Emotion

Neuroscience explains why music moves us even when the lyrics don't.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Lyrics rarely drive the intense emotional resonance we feel for nostalgic music.
  • The "cascading reminiscence bump" allows us to inherit nostalgia from older generations.
  • The brain's default mode network processes profound musical meaning without needing words.
Source: Shaiith / Shutterstock

Recently, I was scrolling through the Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1980. I was 14 years old that year, making it the absolute peak of my "musical reminiscence bump," the developmental window when our brains permanently wire the music of our youth to our deepest emotions.

While perusing the list, I realized there's one song that always stops me dead in my tracks and hits surprisingly hard whenever it catches me off guard in a random place, like a supermarket checkout line. That song is Elton John's "Little Jeannie."

"Little Jeannie" Hits Inexplicably Hard Across Cultures and Generations

Lyrically, this song doesn't say anything profoundly moving until near the end. And the refrain "I want you to be my acrobat, I want you to be my lover" always seems like a throwaway line. On paper, the song could easily be categorized as a seriously schmaltzy, mid-tempo early '80s pop song.

Nevertheless, every time I hear the opening percussion and cascading drum intro, I get verklempt. During the 20-second, lyric-free introduction that might sound like "Muzak-y" elevator music to some, my emotions swell and I'm filled with a deep sense of, for lack of a better word, "wistfulness" that doesn't make sense to me logically.

Curious if I was alone in having such a poignant response to a somewhat cheesy pop song, I looked at the YouTube comments to see if other listeners echoed my sentiment.

Notably, for many of the "Little Jeannie" versions on YouTube, all of which are sung in English by Elton John, the comment sections are dominated by foreign-language responses (lots of Portuguese!). According to Google Translate, these comments convey that even among non-English speakers or ESL listeners, "Little Jeannie" hits hard in bittersweet ways that seem to catch people off guard.

article continues after advertisement

While sifting through various comments, I found two that elucidate the inexplicable power of "Little Jeannie" to stir emotions:

  • "This song makes me ridiculously melancholic for some reason. It can't be nostalgia, this was decades before me. I can't put my finger on it."
  • "Listening to this song always makes me teary-eyed. I really don't know why, because it's not really a sad song. Something about it is just so heart-touching."

Surprisingly, Universal Musical "Scripts" Don't Rely on Lyrics

Why does a song that isn't inherently sad make someone cry? And how can a listener feel nostalgia for an era they didn't live through? As it turns out, the answers lie in a fascinating intersection of behavioral psychology, imagination, and neuroscience.

A new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) on November 16, 2026, investigated the sociocultural dimensions of music-evoked memories. The researchers played 30-second clips of billboard-topping hits to 223 college students, utilizing songs from their own teenage years (the 2010s) and their parents' teenage years (the 1980s and 1990s).

Using natural language processing to analyze the memories these songs evoked, the researchers found that certain songs reliably generated strikingly similar memory scenarios among strangers from comparable backgrounds, driven by culturally learned "scripts."

To find out where that emotion was coming from, the researchers stripped away the music and gave a separate group of participants just a song's lyrics to read. Without music accompanying the words to a song, the shared sociocultural dimensions of people's autobiographical memories and associations diminished.

Based on this observation, the researchers concluded that the lyrics alone don't drive our intense reactions to pop music. Instead, the emotional scripts are embedded in the musical sound and genre itself.

When a YouTube commenter notes that "Little Jeannie" isn't a sad song but makes their eyes well up with tears, it isn't necessarily the lyrics driving that reaction. It's the specific acoustic architecture created by an old Fender Rhodes electric piano, alto saxophone, and flugelhorn, all wrapped in layered vocal harmonies. This unique musical alchemy tugs directly at the heartstrings, completely bypassing the analytical mind where words reside.

Why Songs Often Hit Harder During Adolescence

How does neuroscience explain the enigma of a young listener feeling "ridiculously melancholic" when hearing a song released decades before they were born?

One possible explanation: While we experience a primary surge of memory attachment for the music of our own adolescence, we also develop a secondary attachment to the music of our parents and caregivers from earlier generations. As the authors explain in their recent PNAS paper:

article continues after advertisement

"Interestingly, however, music-evoked autobiographical memories (MEAMs) are characterized by a potentially unique phenomenon known as 'cascading reminiscence bumps,' in which they exhibit a secondary reminiscence bump associated with music that was popular before listeners were born."

As children, we're often captive audiences in the backseat of a car or the family living room. Long before music was siloed into individual earbuds via streaming apps, "hard copy" formats like vinyl records, CDs, and mixtapes filled these shared spaces. Played aloud on common speakers, we passively absorbed our parents' adolescent soundtracks by osmosis.

Yet, even as modern listening habits shift toward isolated headphones, this intergenerational phenomenon persists. This new (2026) study suggests that these cultural "scripts" are so deeply wired into us that even if a younger participant had never heard a specific older song before, their brain can use the song's genre to automatically retrieve a feeling that fits the cultural vibe.

Because these acoustic architectures activate shared neural representations, the emotional script transcends both the generation and the delivery method.

Higher-Order "Meaning" Bypasses Lexical Semantics

Another recent study by Princeton's Elizabeth Margulis and colleagues, published in Nature Communications on August 18, 2026, used fMRI to explore the neural representations of imagined narratives that participants conjured up while listening to unfamiliar music.

During the experiment, researchers scanned people's brains while they listened to completely instrumental tracks. The scans revealed that across different test subjects, the music produced highly organized, shared patterns in the brain's default mode network (DMN). As the authors explain:

"This work demonstrates that music elicits detectable, modality-general representations, a kind of higher-order 'meaning', integrating both narrative imagery and its associated emotional profile, specific to particular excerpts."

article continues after advertisement

Interestingly, Margulis's team found that the DMN doesn't need semantic language to engage in profound meaning-making. This helps to explain why it's almost impossible to pinpoint why certain music evokes shared imagined narratives; these emotions bubble up outside the realm of words (i.e., lexical semantics).

According to the latest 2026 research, music has the power to tap into a cultural frequency that bypasses our critical minds, reminding us that oftentimes, profound meaning is found in things we feel deeply but can't articulate.

item.title: The Power of Play, and Second Chances
item.description:
Play

The Power of Play, and Second Chances

Joy, curiosity, and excitement can open the door to second chances.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Play involves feelings of interest, enjoyment, and surprise.
  • Second chances can refer to any changes in one's life: work, relationships, primary interests, and so on.
  • Understanding feelings, cognition, and language can help in taking advantage of second chances.
Source: New Africa/Adobe Stock

What a strange title—“The Power of Play, and Second Chances”! And yet, the processes underlying play and second chances are linked in important ways. Human development involves three information processing systems: feelings (affects), cognition (thinking, memory, etc.), and language (words to ideas and feelings). Second chances involve all three, but especially feelings.

The Power of Play

Play can be conceptualized as a combination of three of our basic feelings:

  • interest
  • enjoyment
  • surprise

Play is very important in human development and later life. The psychoanalyst Donald Winnicott writes:

“It is in playing and only in playing that the individual child or adult can be creative and to use the whole personality, and it is only in being creative that the individual discovers the self” (1971).

Playing and creating can be seen at all ages and in many activities: art, sports, writing, relationships, psychological treatment, and science. Charles Darwin’s manner when he worked in his 60s was described by his son Francis as bright and animated—play-like!

His love of each particular experiment, and his eager zeal not to lose the fruit of it came out markedly in these crossing experiments—in the elaborate care he took to not make any confusion in putting capsules in the wrong trays, &c. &c. I can recall his appearance as he counted seeds under the simple microscope with an alertness not usually characterizing such mechanical work as counting. I think he personified each seed as a small demon trying to elude him by getting into the wrong heap or jumping away altogether, and this gave to the work the excitement of a game (Browne, 2002).

In everyday language, we are talking about joy, curiosity, and excitement—the wonder of living, and the joy of finding one’s own self through creating.

What Are Second Chances?

Here I use the term second chances to mean a change in any major aspect of one’s life—work, relationships, understanding of one’s self, and so on.

There is much interest in second chances, probably because humans are constantly trying to enhance their lives. Discussions most often focus on work or an important relationship. I know one woman who for years did wonderful work for a financial firm, but she got tired of it. She had always wanted to travel, so she became a flight attendant and traveled the world, with much happiness. And as approximately 40 to 50 percent of first marriages end in divorce over a lifetime, second chances loom large for many people.

One of the best books in this area is Second Chances: Shakespeare and Freud, by literary scholar Stephen Greenblatt and psychoanalyst Adam Phillips. They write:

In the second chance we get, if there is one, there is always, then, the chance of finally realizing our preferred version of ourselves (if you want to picture your ambition for yourself you have to imagine what you would do if you got a second chance). The as-yet unlived life that is our second chance carries what we presume to be our potential. Our second chance must be, at least in prospect, better than our first. It is an opportunity for something to come to life, or to come to more life. It is an opportunity to formulate what we might want for ourselves, and for the other people in our lives. The second chance may begin as a wish—or even as a utopian fantasy—but everything depends on how it is worked out, and on how it works out (2024).

Play and Second Chances

Often in life we come up against boredom, a lack of excitement, or a need for something new and fulfilling—in work, free time, or relationships. What causes a person to consider a second chance, and what leads one to try it or not?

Do fear and shame, or interest (curiosity) and enjoyment rule the day? That really is the question. And its roots run through every developmental phase: childhood, adolescence, early adulthood, adulthood, and older adulthood.

Second chances can be small or large. Small decisions occur all the time, at all ages. The larger dilemmas—picking a school, choice of a mate, work opportunities and changes, and, actually, life and death—arise from adolescence onward. Conscious as well as unconscious factors figure into the outcome, as do our assessments of the past, the present, and fantasies of the future. Feelings, cognition, and language are all involved, but feelings are probably the most important.

Clinically, here is where past and present become especially interesting. Some people get overly excited and jump into things too quickly, and need help using their cognitive processes. But more often we see people with significant feelings of fear and shame who have trouble trying something new because they are protecting themselves from potential hurt or loss.

This is conveyed nicely by the old “car” or “jack” story from years ago.

A person has a flat tire, and he has no jack and can’t fix it. He sees someone across the road who is fixing his tire. He starts across the road to get help, and begins to think—“Wait, I don’t know him…he won’t help me and loan me his jack,” and so on. When he finally reaches the other car, he blurts out tearfully and angrily: “Oh just keep your damn jack,” and stomps away. His past and fears and fantasies have influenced his actions profoundly.

This happens all the time: “These agents won’t like my manuscript.” “This school won’t accept me.”

Fear and shame can seriously undermine the capacity to try something, to speak up. But when we do try and make a mistake, we learn important information about ourselves and how to improve.

The great hockey player Wayne Gretzky put it this way: “You miss 100 percent of the shots you don’t take!”

Wrapping Up

Second chances really mean grappling with small and large decisions, conscious and unconscious, throughout the life cycle. Understanding our basic processing systems—feelings, cognition, and language—can go a long way toward helping us take advantage of them. This is especially true in using interest and enjoyment to counteract fear and shame—and that's the power of play!

item.title: Offbeat Celebrity Crushes: Obsessing Over Nathan Fielder?
item.description:
Media

Offbeat Celebrity Crushes: Obsessing Over Nathan Fielder?

What are the causes of celebrity crushes, both conventional and unconventional?

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Factors such as displays of intimacy, self-disclosure, and vulnerability contribute to developing crushes.
  • Individuals may wonder why they crush on unconventional stars, but psychology offers many explanations.
  • Fantasy is part of desired relationships, both with people in our dialy lives and aspirational others.

The 2026 documentary You Can See Everything is enjoying acclaim, earning very high scores from professional critics (97 percent) and fans (95 percent). In the film, director Nathan Fielder interviews infamous biotech fraudster Elizabeth Holmes and her partner Billy Evans, having been granted close access to the couple, as the title says.

At the same time, there are reports of Fielder’s status as something of a surprise celebrity crush. This isn’t the first time Fielder’s been upheld as an example of an unconventional celebrity crush. He appeared shirtless on the cover of New York magazine in 2022 (2) with the caption “Hot cat dad alert.” The cover story discussed his show The Rehearsal.

Celebrity crushes have been debated as potentially questionable. New York magazine referred to crushes on Fielder, questioning his “inexplicable attractiveness” (1,2).

Parasocial Romantic Relationships

Psychologists call celebrity crushes parasocial romantic relationships, or PSRR for short. Parasocial refers to the idea of the unreality of the relationship because most people who have a crush on a celebrity will never interact with the person, much less date them. If this is the case, why do people have celebrity crushes, including the less conventional ones?

Parasocial relationships of various sorts (friendships and romantic attachments) are mostly carried out in the imagination of the person with the feelings. Often journalists and members of the public do not understand their value. A good way to think about these common feelings is that our fantasies are part of our imagination. Imagining social attachments means playing with the idea of friendship or romance in our own hearts and minds. It has benefits, like being a way to rehearse real relationships and to avoid the downsides of those relationships. There are potential costs such as expecting too much of relationships that don’t fit the ideal of the Hollywood romance or being relatively unimpressed by the looks of regular people.

It’s important to keep in mind that our real relationships also use our imaginations. We fantasize about the crush we have on an office mate, and we imagine telling off the school bully, for example. It may be strange to realize that we probably spend less time actually interacting with real-life romantic partners than we spend daydreaming about interacting with that person. (Daydreaming is very common.)

Offbeat Crush?

What about that so-called offbeat crush? Let’s take the example of Nathan Fielder. Spoiler alert: The following contains references to events in his documentary. First, Nathan Fielder may not look like Chris Hemsworth, but he is still a reasonably attractive man. We may have lost perspective given that Hollywood beauty is extreme. If we saw him in a café in our hometown, we would probably find him attractive. [Note: if you don’t believe me, imagine a picture of an average Walmart shopper in your hometown, and put that next to a picture of Nathan Fielder. Compare and contrast.]

But there are particular aspects of the documentary You Can See Everything that likely increase his appeal. The film is very emotional and has a very noticeable soundtrack designed to heighten feelings. But more than this, there are extreme cues for intimacy and self-disclosure, both of which build and increase attraction.

Can We Talk About the Eye Contact?

If you have seen this documentary or other footage of Elizabeth Holmes, you may have noticed her very unusual eye contact. An expert on lying suggests that this very low blink rate and intense stare is one of her manipulation techniques (3). Looking someone directly in the eye is something people interpret as a sign of honesty. So you can imagine that this kind of unusually intense eye contact is something people fall for. In You Can See Everything, both Elizabeth and Nathan present with this intensity.

Why draw attention to eye contact? Well, in social interactions, eye contact is also a sign of intimacy. What’s more, maintaining eye contact and disclosing highly personal information are indicators of social closeness. Friends tell us their secrets. Intimates look deeply into our eyes. This combination of intimacy and telling secrets might well make us feel close to Nathan, regardless of his motives for using it.

Isn’t It Ironic?

Isn’t it a well-known trope to say that men are bad at sharing their emotions and making themselves vulnerable? So, it follows that someone doing that on a kind of epic scale might be attractive. Taking the idea of vulnerability further, Nathan appears to be charmed by Elizabeth’s manipulation techniques. The film (again, spoilers!) leaves us with the idea that perhaps he’s even fallen in love with her. This is surely an ironic end to a documentary where an interviewer falls for the manipulations of a woman who is known as one of the most epic liars in recent history.

Unexpected or Totally Expected?

Nathan shows a host of other attractive characteristics that are classically crushworthy. Some of these include his intelligence and social status, his bravery in confronting Elizabeth with very difficult questions, and his ability to show both empathy and vulnerability.

We naturally want to attach to desirable individuals. Part of this is based on cultural stories about what makes a desirable mate. The documentary itself plays with some of these cultural stories, for example, in presenting the unconventional love story between Elizabeth Holmes and partner Billy Evans.

Let Me Sum Up

To sum up, crushes on public figures like actors and filmmakers are very normal. Many of us have probably spent time imagining we might meet them and that they would like us. Sometimes a celebrity crush might seem unconventional, but we should keep in mind the crazy high standards of Hollywood beauty and the host of other characteristics we find appealing. Things like an ability to be vulnerable and open, to be brave, and to demonstrate your ability to stare unblinkingly into another person’s eyes are things that will catch and hold our attention.

Whether or not you are crushing on Nathan Fielder, Elizabeth Holmes, or any celebrity, the documentary You Can See Everything is a (fever?) dream of sorts for anyone interested in the psychology of human social interactions, especially at the extremes. You’ve probably never seen anything quite like it. If you have a chance to catch it, I hope it inspires some interesting conversations for you.

item.title: AI Is My Best Collaborator Ever
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI Is My Best Collaborator Ever

AI has enabled me to build a company alone.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • AI's vast information and my knowledge, experience, perspective, and wisdom make for a winning combination.
  • AI is always available, can carry a heavy workload, is incredibly productive, and costs very little.
  • AI has no ego or emotions.
  • AI can't share the human experience of collective accomplishment.
Source: AI generated; Jim Taylor, Ph.D.

I have historically not played (or worked) particularly well with others. Why? I’m an introvert, prodigiously productive, and have exceptionally high standards of quality. And I like to be in control. This is great for me professionally, but it doesn’t make for the best collaboration.

The media is full of stories about the various evils of AI: environmental degradation, economic upheaval, depersonalization, job losses, infrastructure costs, AI slop, political manipulation, ethical concerns, and uncontrolled oligarchs.

I’m not an "AI will change the world only for the good" evangelist. But my collaboration with ChatGPT (Chat for short) has been a truly amazing experience, and I would like to share it.

My company is developing an app based on my decades of experience in psychology. I bring the substantive knowledge, intellectual property, and vision. Chat helps close the gap in my technological and financial limitations without spending tens of thousands of dollars on an app development team or waiting months for the app to be built.

Knowledge and What AI Can Do With It

I’ve spent decades accumulating knowledge, experience, perspective, and, hopefully, some wisdom in psychology. Yet my expertise occupies a relatively small corner of the world’s knowledge. Building a company requires me to venture beyond it. With Chat, I can discuss app navigation and marketing strategy without finding a different expert for every question.

Availability, Workload, and Cost

I work best on my own schedule. When I have an idea or run into a problem, I want to work on it right away.

Chat is always available. It doesn’t sleep, eat, exercise, socialize, or have family responsibilities. I can talk to it in the morning and continue in the evening. No scheduling meetings. And don’t even get me started about the challenges posed by vastly different time zones.

Chat can work on several tasks at once with its subagents. It doesn’t get hungry, tired, bored, stressed, annoyed, or discouraged. And this is all for a fraction of the cost of hiring a team of experts.

Getting Sh*t Done

I have always valued GSD: getting sh*t done. Dreams are great, but they are worth nothing unless you bring them to life. Chat gets sh*t done as quickly and as well as I do, sometimes better. A question can be answered in minutes instead of requiring hours of research.

Chat’s responses are structured, which is how I think. It organizes information, lists steps, and explains complex concepts simply, which is especially helpful in unfamiliar territory.

Chat and I have repeatedly moved from describing how something should work to a workable version in hours or days rather than weeks or months. And, boy, is that satisfying.

A Sounding Board

Creativity and innovation involve both the evolution and revolution of thought. Ideas can develop logically, step by step, or spontaneously, in a moment of insight. Chat keeps up with the pace, range, and chaos of my thinking.

I present a raw idea. Chat offers a perspective that prompts further thought. I challenge a suggestion. It offers an alternative. We develop the idea until it can be put into practice. Deciding how my app guides users to content, for example, takes our discussions between psychology, language, design, and functionality.

Learning How I Work

Chat has become remarkably adept at understanding how I think and express myself. I can provide examples of my writing, explain why a phrase doesn’t sound like me, or specify vocabulary for the app.

A clear instruction can produce an immediate improvement. And, yes, Chat helped me write this article. Excluding it would seem odd.

No Ego or Emotions

With a Ph.D. in psychology, I know how ego and emotions complicate collaboration. Frustration, fear, jealousy, insecurity, defensiveness, and impatience can interfere with even the most capable people, including me.

I can reject Chat’s ideas, criticize its work, request another revision, or express annoyance without offending it. I don’t need to protect its feelings to preserve our working relationship.

It doesn’t need praise or recognition. Nor does it experience self-doubt, self-criticism, or fear of failure. My own ego and emotions, on the other hand, remain fully operational!

The Limitations Are Real

The collaboration is far from frictionless. I often stare at my screen wondering how this capable tool can be so imperfect and infuriating.

First, Chat can confidently provide information that is plain wrong. These hallucinations are especially problematic outside my expertise. I recognize a poor explanation of psychology more readily than one of software development.

Second, it can be excessively agreeable; yes, the whole sycophant thing. I need accurate information, clear feedback, and disagreement when warranted. I have instructed it to avoid flattery and challenge my thinking, but how effective this is remains to be seen.

Third, it forgets things. We establish a way of working, then find it missing in a subsequent version. Repeating instructions is frustrating when consistency is essential to our product.

Fourth, Chat goes down rabbit holes. One unsuccessful fix leads to another, ad nauseam, ad infinitum, in an extended game of whack-a-mole. Truly infuriating. I’ve learned to interrupt those rabbit holes and get it back on track. Amazingly, despite its mistakes, Chat always finds the solution that enables us to move forward.

Using AI is like driving a car. However much it can do, I still have to keep my hands on the steering wheel (though that has already begun to change with cars and AI).

What I Still Miss

Despite my awe and, dare I say, reverence toward Chat, one limitation matters differently. I still value sharing the experience of creating something meaningful with someone. When an intractable problem is solved, or an idea becomes reality, wow, that’s why I do what I do.

Chat can acknowledge a milestone and the effort involved. It cannot share my sense of purpose, feel proud of what we’ve built, or revel in the accomplishment. That absence is palpable.

For all the ways AI suits me, I’m still human. I want other people to share in creating something of value and feel the same sense of purpose.

Chat is my best collaborator ever. It helps me think more expansively, work more productively, and create something I couldn’t on my own, at comparatively little cost. Yet it has clarified something I may have undervalued. There is great satisfaction in getting the work done. But there is something very human about sharing why it matters.

item.title: Use AI Last, Not First
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Use AI Last, Not First

The urge to reach for AI first is misleading. Use it last instead.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • AI seems like the first go-to for all our problems, but that may not be the best route to creative solutions.
  • Writing down your own ideas before engaging with AI boosts recall and creative activation.
  • Reframing problems by removing assumptions can unlock clearer, more innovative solutions.

Most of us today do the same thing the moment a problem lands on our lap. Almost automatically, we open the chat window and pull up our favorite AI tool. Then we type in our prompt. Seconds later, a rather reasonable-appearing answer appears on the screen.

It feels like a win. Yet it’s not.

The problem isn’t that AI gives bad answers. It’s that AI seems like the easy way out. But it's deceptive, depriving us of the opportunity to use our human creative abilities to solve problems in new and novel ways.

AI cannot live in the now; it exists only as a snapshot of history and a crawl of data and the internet. That history cannot come up with ideas right now. And it turns out that right now is when you need the fresh ideas the most, to solve issues that are plaguing you. AI can only take a very narrow view of the past and try deceptively to apply it to the future.

So before you reach for AI first—because after all, AI is making everyone’s ideas the same anyhow—reach for it last. Here are some ideas for pushing back on the use of AI and instead relying on your own abilities to solve problems.

1. Go First

Instead of reaching for AI first, you go first. Write down three ideas that you have for the problem that just fell into your lap.

But the twist?

Write down the three worst ideas you can possibly come up with. Instead of pressing yourself to get it right from the get-go, stretch your solution mindset to think of issues creatively without the pressure to get it right.

Then take a stab at three ideas that will actually solve the problem. You may see some cross-pollination from the worst ideas list too.

In a recent MIT Media Lab experiment1, people who wrote down ideas first and then later switched to AI showed higher recall and activation. People who started with AI and then wrote on their own? They showed under-engagement.

Write down your ideas with a pen and paper first—old school. It turns out that doing it the old way may be more likely to make creativity and more lucid thinking2 happen for you.

2. Turn Prompt Time Into Bored Time

I have friends in various industries who literally brag to me about the time they spend on their AI prompts. They say things like, “Nir—if you spend an extra five minutes on each prompt you put in, the AI answer is so much better.” I even have a friend who dedicates 15 minutes or more to each prompt. Every day.

Yet no matter how long you spend prompting the AI, you still get AI answers that sound much the same as the answers everyone else is getting. Instead, turn prompt time into being bored time.

Monitor the time you spend on AI each week asking it to do things for you. At the end of the week, see how much time you were on AI, and instead shift that time to being bored. So if it’s 20 minutes a week or 40 minutes a week, use that time differently. Plot down a 40-minute block of time during the week and call it “me time.” And then, instead of prompting an AI, be bored. Creativity and innovation will flow.

The research backs this. Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman3 found that experiencing a state of boredom increases creative potential, idea generation, and problem-solving performance.

So take the time you would waste on AI and invest it in yourself instead – the ideas you make while bored can be life-changing.

3. Untangle Complexity

Chances are the problem that fell into your lap is rife with assumptions. Some of the assumptions are ones that you had made, some may be from a coworker, some may be from your ignorance of nuance, and some may just be stubborn histories.

Instead of getting bogged down with complexity, write the central problem on a piece of paper and then cross out all the assumptions made.

This process will bring clarity to an otherwise emotional or difficult problem by eliminating the assumptions that are preloaded into the problem. It also reframes the original problem in a simpler way, allowing you to solve it without all the extra fat and weight.

Technion professors Ronen, Goldschmidt, and Erez4 studied how people interpret a problem while solving it, which they call problem structuring. They found that extra clarity helped mainly because people used it to rethink the problem itself. How you frame the problem matters, not just the time you put in.

Overall, our urge to go to AI first for all our issues is a fallacy. We may think it's faster, cheaper, and better, but like all things that seem too good to be true, it is. If instead we try the three ideas listed above and then turn to AI as a last resort, we can begin to strengthen our creative problem-solving core to allow for new and novel ideas that no AI can ever generate.

item.title: 12 Features of the Experience of Addiction
item.description:
Addiction

12 Features of the Experience of Addiction

A less clinical description of the many dimensions of addiction.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Addiction is a full-bodied condition that imposes limitations on people.
  • Addiction always brings negative consequences; there are no positive addictions.
  • Addiction is a personal, interpersonal, political, and even communal condition.
  • It is not possible to “addiction-proof” people, although some may have some access to protective features.

Do all addictions share one defining feature or characteristic? I tend to think not, and instead argue that addictions are better understood as having a family resemblance. Members of an extended family may not share one trait but rather a host of traits that overlap, crisscross, and connect the individuals. With addiction, there are patterns and weaves that connect the behaviors classified as addictions.

Here are 12 features or dimensions that I believe to be common characteristics of addiction.

Addiction is one way that a person can lose themselves. The loss can take multiple forms depending on the individual, the substance they use or behaviors in which they engage, and the contexts in which they live.

Addiction is a condition that imposes some limitations on people. Based on a wealth of data from my own experiences, I am certain that I cannot drink socially. I may be OK for a while, but I have good reason to believe that my drinking will pick up steam like a runaway locomotive. This certainty is bedrock for me and enables me to impose limitations on my own actions. I don’t go into bars even if you tell me that it’s a restaurant that serves drinks. I know a bar that sells food when I see it, and I am not going in it.

As I have gotten older and spent more time living in recovery, I’ve come to see that there is freedom within limitations. Too often we assume that having limitations imposes constraints that make us less free. This is true to some degree, but it obscures an important dimension of freedom.

Many philosophers would say that absolute freedom of choice is utterly terrifying; we humans would overload on the possibility and choice. I get overwhelmed trying to select a particular Triscuit cracker I want now that there are about 20 versions of that classic cracker. Getting overwhelmed by choices often leads to bad decisions.

A defining feature of addiction is that there are always negative consequences. This is a necessary condition. Addictions take time to develop. While early on, use may bring some benefit, at some point, the costs to a person become greater than the benefits.

Addiction is a multilevel condition with personal, interpersonal, and broader social dimensions. On the personal level, it is the person—not their brain—that is addicted. Within a person, it is a biochemical condition where drugs and certain behaviors affect functions of the brain but also different organs and systems.

Addiction is a full-bodied condition. My hangovers lasted days, often causing terrible nausea, shakes, and blurred vision among a host of physical ailments. When not drinking straight out of a bottle but out of a glass, my right hand always held the glass and swirled the contents around. I still catch myself doing that when served seltzer in a short glass. It brings me right back. The smell of beer turns my head while the smell of red wine turns my stomach. Our bodies hold memories and meanings.

There are important psychological dimensions to addiction as well. How we feel about ourselves and the beliefs we hold affect our use, which in turn affects how we regard ourselves. Addiction shapes our sense of self and how we see ourselves in the world.

For some, addiction is a spiritual condition, where drugs and behaviors try to fill a void or create meaning that seems to be missing.

Addiction is also a moral condition in which certain moral goods such as dignity, self-respect, care for our own selves and others, friendship, and flourishing are harmed. To claim addiction is a moral condition is not to claim it is a moral failure.

Addiction is also an interpersonal phenomenon. We humans are social creatures who are always in multiple relationships with family, friends, colleagues, neighbors, and other community members. Some of these are intentionally and freely chosen; others are a matter of circumstance or chance.

For many, the use of alcohol or other drugs made social interactions easier—at least at the beginning. Most of us learned how to use with others. We may have had drinking or using buddies, and many of our social interactions may have revolved around our use. When we progressed past a certain point, others may have cut us off, or we pruned people from our lives who questioned our use.

Addiction is a political phenomenon as well. By “political” I don’t mean electoral politics but the way that power flows through all the dimensions of our lives and communities. Power shapes the choices that some people face.

We are all free to quit paid employment, for example, but if we need to work to support ourselves or our families, or because we need insurance, we are free in theory rather than in practice. Also, we may feel compelled to adjust our careers or other significant life choices because of what others want for us or what society expects of us. Thus, we face all sorts of political or power pressures each day and try to make the best decisions possible.

Sometimes, we are caught between a rock and a hard place on the political level, and this may lead to unhealthy or bad decisions on both the personal and interpersonal levels.

In one sense, addiction is an equal opportunity condition; no one is immune to it. No one can be “addiction-proofed.”

In another sense, addiction is a very unequal opportunity condition. Some will have more social, economic, or educational protective layers that enable them to head off a problem before it gets really bad or to mitigate the bad consequences of their use. Others who lack these protective features and insulating layers may be subject to many more stressors and pay a much steeper price for their behaviors.

All of these dimensions—personal, interpersonal, and political—overlap and crisscross, creating a very dense fabric of tangled issues. This dense tangle can contribute to the development of an addiction.

item.title: Why Men Ghost Their Therapists
item.description:
Therapy

Why Men Ghost Their Therapists

Pushing for vulnerable disclosure can force male clients out of therapy.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Men need counseling, but many do not seek it or stay long enough to get the help they need.
  • Nearly 45 percent of men in one survey left therapy, often because they did not connect with the therapist.
  • Counselors can help men stay by building safety before pushing for vulnerable emotional disclosure.
Source: RDNE Stock Project/Pexels

Counseling men is not like counseling women. If you try to counsel a man like a woman, it can quickly blow up—not with a bang, but a whimper. That male client may likely drop out. This is not to say that all men or all women are alike. It is to say that male gender-role socialization can shape what men need from counseling and how they engage with it.

A Female-Dominated Field

This mismatch is understandable—women are the majority. More counselors, counseling clients, and counselor educators are women. Women made up 74.5 percent of the Bureau of Labor Statistics category “counselors, all other” in 2025 (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2026). Women made up 80.2 percent of students and 68.6 percent of full-time faculty in Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs-accredited counseling programs in 2024 (2025). Women were also more likely than men to receive counseling or therapy in 2024—16.9 percent compared with 10.9 percent (Briones and Villarroel, 2026).

Counseling is a female-dominated field, which is interesting because it was not always this way. Among faculty members in accredited counseling programs who earned their degrees in the 1960s and 1970s, only 26.7 percent were women. Five decades later, 63 percent were women (Baggerly and colleagues, 2017).

Men Need Counseling, but They Do Not Stay

Men desperately need mental health support, but they are less likely than women to access counseling services (Briones and Villarroel, 2026). Yet, men die by suicide at nearly four times the rate of women (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2026). Men also have higher drug-overdose death rates. In a federal analysis of deaths involving fentanyl, methamphetamine, cocaine, heroin, and oxycodone, the death rate was higher for men for every drug examined (Spencer and colleagues, 2023).

When men do attend counseling, many drop out. In a survey of 1,907 Australian men who had attended therapy, 44.8 percent reported dropping out. Among the men classified as dropouts, 26.6 percent attended only once and did not return. The most common reason was a lack of connection with the therapist (Seidler and colleagues, 2021).

Men need counseling, but they do not stay; a reason may be engagement. Men do not always engage with counseling when they enter services. This may happen because counselors assume male clients think, behave, and have treatment needs like female clients. But they do not always have the same needs.

Do Not Rush Vulnerability

Counselors get it wrong. They expect men to disclose emotionally vulnerable information at the outset of counseling. But vulnerable emotional disclosure can be difficult for men. Male gender-role socialization may not teach some men how to identify and express emotions, and it may associate vulnerable emotional disclosure with weakness. Specific messages associated with traditional masculinity, such as “no complaining,” “boys don’t cry,” and “pull yourself up by your bootstraps,” send the message to boys, who then become men, that they need to shut down their feelings, not share or open up about their struggles, and avoid seeking help (Levant and Parent, 2019; Seidler and colleagues, 2016).

For some men, the counseling office is unfamiliar and foreign. They feel like a fish out of water. If a counselor expects men to be vulnerable and disclose how they feel, the counselor may believe they are getting to the real issue. Yet the male client may experience it as being pushed into risky waters before rapport and safety have been built.

Start in the Safe Zone

Counselors need to tread lightly. They should start the relationship in the safe zone, often at a more intellectual or practical level, until the man feels more comfortable and safety has been established. Counselors can ask what is happening, what needs to change, what the man has already tried, and what he wants from counseling.

This does not mean avoiding emotions or allowing the client to remain emotionally distant forever. It is a starting point. The focus is on pacing the work we do with men, where we progressively build up to emotional disclosure. A review of strategies for engaging men found support for collaborative, transparent, action-oriented, and goal-focused approaches. This also accounts for masculine socialization (Seidler and colleagues, 2018). Once the man feels that the counselor understands him and that the relationship is safe, they can move together into deeper, riskier waters.

Men need counseling. But getting men into counseling is only the first step. Counselors can also build strong connections that encourage clients to stay.

item.title: From Medical Marijuana to Marijuana Everywhere
item.description:
Cannabis

From Medical Marijuana to Marijuana Everywhere

Compassion, legalization, and commercialization reshaped the cannabis market.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Unproven medical claims helped commercialize alcohol, cocaine, tobacco, and now cannabis.
  • Marijuana legalization created powerful commercial interests far beyond compassionate medical use.
  • Frequent cannabis users, including those with addiction, drive most sales, while illegal markets persist.
  • We need to protect nonusers from secondhand and thirdhand cannabis smoke and its potential health risks.

This is Part 1 of a two-part series.

Walk through almost any American city, and you’ll likely smell marijuana smoke. Nonsmokers are complaining the most. Sidewalks. Hotels. Apartment buildings. Public spaces. Marijuana seems to be everywhere.

How did we get here?

The modern medical marijuana movement gained momentum when patients with cancer, AIDS, and other serious illnesses sought relief. Compassion was a powerful argument for this group. So was criminal justice reform because sometimes penalties for possessing small amounts of marijuana were unreasonably high. But neither compassion nor decriminalization established that marijuana was effective for one illness, let alone dozens of diseases. Evidence supports certain cannabinoid-based treatments for rare indications, but not the safety or efficacy of cannabis dispensary products.

Not '60s Marijuana
Source: Mark Gold, MD, with permission

A systematic review by Petrilli and colleagues found higher-potency cannabis was associated with increased risks of psychosis and cannabis use disorder (CUD).

Alcohol, cocaine, and tobacco were promoted as medicines too.
Source: Mark Gold, MD, with permission

How Marijuana Legalization Changed the Market

It started with the 1996 medical marijuana ballot measure in California, Proposition 215.

In 2012, Colorado and Washington became the first states to approve recreational marijuana legalization through statewide ballot initiatives.

Promises made to gain citizen support included fewer arrests, less illicit dealing, and medical benefits. There were also promises of tax revenue. Legalization also created retailers who need customers and investors expecting returns. Governments collect taxes and need money.

Recommendations for responsible cannabis commercialization.
Source: Mark Gold, MD, with permission

Kevin Sabet and Big Marijuana

Kevin Sabet, PhD, and former Congressman Patrick Kennedy cofounded Smart Approaches to Marijuana (SAM) in 2013. They are advocates, but research has supported many of their policy suggestions.

One study analyzed 187,573 survey responses between 2018 and 2023. They raised questions about marketing practices, especially those reaching children. Xu and colleagues subsequently reported associations between cannabis advertising, price-based promotions, and initiation among adolescents and young adults.

Rotering and Apollonio also documented cannabis-industry lobbying concerning indoor smoking exemptions and pregnancy warnings.

Didn't we already learn these lessons from Big Tobacco?

Cannabis Revenue: Who’s Driving Sales?

Legal U.S. cannabis sales reached an estimated $29.1 billion in 2025, with industry projections anticipating further growth in 2026. But tax revenue isn’t the same as public health benefits.

Perhaps the most important finding about commercial cannabis is not how much is sold, but who’s buying it.

Cigarette manufacturers also depend on nicotine-dependent smokers. A disproportionate share of alcohol sales come from heavy drinkers. Fast-food and ultra-processed food companies benefit from frequent consumption. The marijuana industry is similar in this way. A study of Washington State's cannabis market estimated daily or near-daily consumers accounted for 91 percent of the market in 2016.

Reducing heavy cannabis consumption would reduce industry revenue and state tax receipts.

Did Legalization Eliminate the Illegal Market?

Approximately 62 percent of cannabis consumed in California during 2024 came from illicit sources.

The legal market expanded, but the illegal market remains as substantial as ever. Illegal cannabis products may be cheaper because producers and sellers avoid taxes, testing requirements, licensing fees, and other regulatory costs while offering anonymity and home or street delivery, providing a competitive advantage.

From Hippie Marijuana of the 1960s to High-Potency THC

The marijuana smoked during the 1960s is not the cannabis sold in today's dispensaries. Historical estimates suggest marijuana in the 1960s often contained 1 percent THC or less. By the early 1990s, concentrations were around 3 percent, rising to approximately 4 percent in 1995. It did not stop there.

By 2014, average THC potency reached approximately 12 percent. By 2022, the DEA reported an average of 16 percent THC in monitored marijuana plants. Today's commercial flower may contain 20 to 30 percent THC, while concentrated products such as wax, shatter, and oils may contain 60 to 90 percent.

The dose escalation in potency over time is undeniable. No one today can say, as experts did in the ‘60s, that marijuana isn’t ever addicting, and today, addiction is more likely than ever.

Petrilli and colleagues' systematic review linked higher-potency cannabis with increased risks of psychosis and cannabis use disorder.

We didn’t legalize the marijuana of the '60s. We commercialized highly potent, concentrated forms of THC, without the long-term safety studies or FDA evidence expected of medicines.

But shouldn't people who never used cannabis receive protections comparable to those established for nonsmokers of tobacco? This is the most neglected question in cannabis public health, proving we are in a collective denial.

Secondhand smoke is firsthand smoke without consent.

Back to the Future

Today, cigarette smoke is treated like poison, but cannabis smoke enters apartments, office buildings, hotel rooms, shared ventilation systems, and public spaces. Neighbors complain because they smell it. Sometimes they cannot escape it.

Cannabis smoke contains fine particulate matter (PM₂.₅), carbon monoxide, volatile organic compounds, and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. The CDC warns secondhand cannabis smoke contains toxic and cancer-causing chemicals also present in tobacco smoke, sometimes at comparable or higher concentrations.

Cannabis does not contain nicotine, but cannabis smoke contains something tobacco smoke does not: THC. Controlled experiments in humans by Herrmann and colleagues demonstrated secondhand cannabis smoke exposure can produce measurable blood THC concentrations in poorly ventilated environments. They also reported secondhand exposure could produce subjective psychoactive effects.

Tripathi and colleagues studied 275 children and reported cannabis smoking inside the home was associated with approximately fivefold higher odds of evidence of cannabis in the body and brain by detecting urinary cannabinoid biomarkers. This doesn’t establish intoxication or addiction, but raises an obvious question: Why should children be exposed to THC-containing smoke?

Also, uncertainty about the magnitude of harm doesn’t prove repeated exposure is safe for children or adults.

Thirdhand Exposure

Tobacco research taught homeowners, renters, hotel guests, and the rest of us another lesson: Smoke doesn’t disappear when the cigarette, joint, or bong goes out.

Tobacco researchers showed persistent residues in indoor environments. These alarming findings elevated concerns about infants' and young children's safety. Smoke-related combustion products remain on furniture, carpeting, clothing, walls, and household dust. Some residues can transfer or be resuspended. This is thirdhand smoke.

A 2025 JAMA Cardiology study by Mohammadi and colleagues reported associations between chronic marijuana smoking or THC-edible use (gummies, food including marijuana, such as the classic marijuana brownies) and impaired vascular endothelial function.

Who Pays for Cannabis Costs?

What about emergency department visits? Cannabis use disorder? Anhedonia? Psychosis? Cannabis hyperemesis syndrome, characterized by recurrent episodes of severe nausea and vomiting? Asthma, impaired driving? Treatment costs? Costs may include addiction treatment, psychiatric and medical emergencies, the impacts of impaired driving, environmental exposure, and other health consequences.

We need prospective studies beginning before first cannabis use and continuing over time. We need to measure potential benefits and harms of legalization. We then need to use the FDA to establish medicinal benefit and calculate the risk-benefit balance.

Conclusion

Legalization, while circumventing science and the FDA, does not make marijuana safe. Slick marketing does not make it medicine. Nothing justifies exposing others to smoke.

The lessons of tobacco, alcohol, and cocaine should not be forgotten: Public health must come before commercial interests.

The next post in this series will examine the neuroscience of THC and the addiction, pregnancy, and prevention lessons we should already be applying.

item.title: Wait, What? The Moon Landing Was Faked?
item.description:
Conspiracy Theories

Wait, What? The Moon Landing Was Faked?

Five reasons that people credit celebrities' crackpot theories.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Celebrity is easily confused with expertise.
  • Conspiracy theories simplify and soothe, sometimes, however, with sinister effect.
  • People are entitled to their own opinions, but not to their own facts.

Imagine that at an upcoming holiday gathering you have been cornered and obliged to entertain a preposterous theory. Pick from a few of these tales that have circulated:

  • A team of clever special-effects artists staged the Apollo 11 moon landing. How else can you explain that the American flag that the “astronauts” planted (plainly actors in a studio!) waved in the moon’s vacuum?
  • A pope fabricated a span of centuries in the Middle Ages to spin the calendar ahead so that the year 1,000 and its prophetic, millennialist vision could triumph during his lifetime. So, OK then, you ask, what about the Bayeux Tapestry and all that prepared for the Battle of Hastings? Well, isn’t that simply the so-called 11th-century version of breaking fake news?
  • And one more, from the vast store of folk remedy purveyed for profit on social media: Imagine you’re overhearing a conversation about the virtues of vaginal steaming to “balance hormones.” Let me guess, at this point you are squirming away to sample the reindeer-shaped cheese ball.

Celebrity Endorsements and Assorted Goop

Now put names to the adherents to these outlandish ideas. In media appearances, New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye, along with none other than hometown hero Josh Allen, have expressed skepticism about the moon landing. To be fair, it’s hard to know if they were just playing around. The late NFL star Jared Lorenzen was also a moon landing skeptic, a view he had held ever since watching a conspiracy video in college. Professional basketball stars share the notion, and so have some Hollywood actors.

Moving further out, retired chess grandmaster Garry Kasparov supports the notion that our calendar is missing 300 years of history. To Kasparov and other adherents, written history arose around 800 A.D., not around 5,000 years ago as everybody thinks. The ancient history of Rome and Greece is therefore an elaborate forgery meant to suppress a true chronology of Slavic world supremacy.

And as for folk remedies gone viral—perching atop a steaming pot infused with mugwort, for instance—gynecologists warned, unsurprisingly, that the practice may result in accidental burns. California prosecutors slapped Goop, the lucrative company owned by Gwyneth Paltrow (a proponent of “yoni steaming” and other practices, including inserting jade eggs), with fines over false medical claims.

Mischief, Misinformation, and Delusion

It is easy to list passionate and strange celebrity beliefs that range from mischief and marketing to misinformation and delusion.

Dan Aykroyd, of "Ghostbusters" fame, markets Crystal Head Vodka as “enlightened drinking.”
Source: Dustintitus/Wikimedia Commons (2017)/CC BY-SA 4.0

Dan Aykroyd, of Ghostbuster fame, for example, tells the story that aliens have strategically seeded 13 crystal skulls on the planet. (He playfully markets his line of Crystal Head Vodka as “enlightened drinking.”) Kylie Jenner, famous for being from a famous family but not for biochemistry, thinks that jet contrails are really “chemtrails” that have caused honeybee declines. (Spoiler alert: They aren’t, and they haven’t.) Madonna, who perpetually wars with her Roman Catholic upbringing and dabbles in mystical number combinations, wears a red string bracelet as “spiritual protection.” (She claims this is “science.”) Kanye West, who has a publicly acknowledged history of bipolar disorder, famously became convinced that vaccines contain microchips.

In the modern media ecosphere, it is sometimes difficult to separate the “not-serious” from the “un-serious” and make-believe from marketing.

Why Do We Pay Attention to What Celebrities Think?

Finding eccentric, far-fetched beliefs is not difficult. It is harder, though, to figure out why we should listen to celebrities’ pronouncements.

After all, we can effortlessly consult qualified opinions from credentialed experts. This is an enormous luxury. With a click, without visiting a library or cracking a book, we can find reliable information in disciplines such as history, cognitive psychology, medicine, ecology, chemistry, astrophysics, mathematics, engineering, and so on.

Here are five explanations of why conspiratorial claptrap persists.

  1. In with the in-crowd. It took nearly 2,000 years before scientists (Copernicus, Brahe, Galileo), who were at risk of clerical torture, overcame the orthodox view that the sun, planets, and stars revolved around the earth. The orthodox view had required incredibly complex and unlikely celestial gymnastics, yet the “argument from authority”—the venerable Aristotle’s authority—long prevailed. Now bucking an improbable but popular notion risks only ghosting on social media.
  2. Oops. Sometimes prominent people who rely on their limited observations make simple mistakes. Confirmation bias inspires claims like those that retired football star Tom Brady as well as fashion designer and former pop singer Victoria Beckham hold—that “alkaline water” lowers blood pH and therefore makes them healthier, stronger, and keener. This is simply a mistake. No question they both look robust and energized, but that can probably be chalked up not to blood chemistry, but to exercise, rest, abjuring smoking and alcohol, and sticking to a healthy menu packed with fruits, nuts, and vegetables. Plus (possibly) some cosmetic treatments.
  3. Blithe ignorance. Alabama congressman Mo Brooks bravely toed the party line on global warming denial. In 2018, in a hearing of the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, Brooks insisted that the rise in sea level was owed not to meltwater from retreating glaciers but to erosion. “What about the White Cliffs of Dover?” he asked, and what about “cliffs crashing into the sea?” There’s your explanation for coastal flooding! The folksy representative, underprepared in climate science, plainly had not mastered enough information to grasp all that he could not understand or care about. Psychologists and philosophers call this the Dunning-Kruger Effect—not knowing enough to know what you do not know.
  4. The halo effect. Media saturation makes famous people seem trustworthy, and celebrity is confused with expertise. When a former Playboy model appeared on Oprah Winfrey’s program to argue passionately that vaccines cause autism, public health measures suffered. Her contention rested on a myth based on fraudulent research. Parasocial trust, a kind of sanctification, often joins a low appetite for critical thinking.
  5. Comfort and control. Unexamined beliefs offer protection against the onslaughts of a chaotic, complicated, threatening world. Conspiracy theories simplify and soothe. Their most sinister expressions arise as scapegoating. Adherents find perverse comfort in blaming a vulnerable group. Alas, history and current events supply plenty of examples where underprepared people have made themselves sitting ducks for conspiratorial thinking that victimizes others.

So, was Old Glory fluttering on the moon? Nope. The flag merely hung on a rod, gathered like a shower curtain. As the scholarly senator Daniel Patrick Moynihan wittily observed, “Everyone is entitled to his own opinion, but not to his own facts.”

item.title: The Meaning and Value of Stress
item.description:
Stress

The Meaning and Value of Stress

Our response to stressors determines our outcome; reframing is the key.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Stress has been presented to us as a damaging reaction to uncontrollable external forces.
  • Decades of stress research have found that our stress response is necessary and strengthening.
  • Reframing our stress response as a valuable marker of meaning and resilience can improve our lives.
Source: Otra Ruta / Pexels

For the last 60 years or so, we've been warned about stress and told to do everything we can to avoid it.

We've been taught how to meditate our way out of stress, down-regulate from it, "hack our cortisol," reduce our adrenaline, manage our vagus nerve, calm ourselves, numb ourselves, distract ourselves, and halt our stress responses in as many ways as we can.

We've also been taught to view many of the difficulties in our lives as always-negative exterior forces, or stressors, that act upon us without our knowledge or permission. Stress has been presented to us as a dangerously unwanted thing with no value whatsoever.

Thankfully, newer research into stressors and our stress response has found the opposite to be true.

The Healing Nature of Stress

In part 1 of this series, I focused on the weasel word of stress, because our stress response is an emotional response. In my work, Dynamic Emotional Integration, I help people understand the emotions that form the foundation of our stress response. We learn how to name these emotions with precision and work directly with them to access the essential intelligence they contribute to us.

Three of the main emotions I see in our stress response are: anxiety (the emotion of motivation and task completion), anger (which helps us identify and uphold what we value), and panic (which steps forward when our lives are in danger).

Each of these emotions helps us meet stressors with intelligence and focus. When we know which emotions are supporting us, and we know how to work with those emotions (instead of against them), stressful situations can teach us who we are, what's important to us, and how we can meet life's challenges with focus, skills, and resilience.

But if we don't know how to identify or work with our emotions, we may feel overwhelmed as our bodies increase our activation to help us meet the necessary stressors we face. We may also learn two unhelpful lessons:

  1. We may mistakenly view stressors as alien or uncontrollable.
  2. We may treat our natural emotional responses as problems instead of valuable tools.

If we believe that stressors are foreign and that our emotions are problems, we'll create unnecessary suffering, not just in response to the stressors but because our skills are missing in action.

Reframing Our Stress Response to Access Its Genius

Psychological researcher Kelly McGonigal has been focusing on stress for many years, and in her 2016 book, The Upside of Stress: Why Stress Is Good for You, and How to Get Good at It, she shares information from decades of stress research. Her book is full of surprising facts that turn our understanding of stress on its ear. For instance:

We Only "Stress Out" About Things That Mean Something to Us

If I told you that the price of tiger chow has gone up by 40 percent, you might have little to no reaction (assuming you aren't a tiger keeper). This is a big price increase, but because it has no meaning to you and does not impact any part of your life, your stress response will be quiet—as it should be; there's nothing for you to do about this, and your emotions don't need to be involved.

But if I told you that your share of the cost for your child's monthly doctor's visits has gone up by 40 percent, it's likely that your stress response would engage. Your emotions, most notably anxiety and anger, might intensify to bring you the energy and focus you need to work the problem. Your stress response would help you know that this situation is important, that it's worth your time and focus, and that you need its increased energy to help you make new plans to support your child's well-being.

Sadly, most stress management approaches would have you try to calm yourself or suppress your emotions (or merely observe them), as if the activation you feel is a problem in and of itself. But this old, tired idea is not only wrong; it's counterproductive, because the strength of your stress response is a key to your success and even mastery of the situation.

A Higher Stress Response Is Correlated to a Stronger Resilience Arc

Of all the surprising things in stress research, this may be the most delightful: The strength of your stress response—your emotional intensity, your hyper-focus, your "nerves"—is directly connected to your ability to thrive. And this continues to be true even when you're well-acquainted with a stressor and no longer see it as surprising or shocking.

Researchers studied new and seasoned skydivers, certain that they would see a reduced stress response (reduced cortisol, adrenaline, and heart rate, less "stress") as the skydivers became accustomed to throwing themselves out of planes. Strangely, there wasn't any reduction in the markers of stress in the seasoned skydivers; in fact, the most skilled skydivers continued to exhibit very high stress responses, often higher than people jumping out of planes for the first time.

What they did find was that the seasoned skydivers had reframed their stress responses as excitement, readiness, stimulation, and even zest for life. This reframing helped them treat their activation as a necessary and fun part of skydiving, even though they might have experienced the exact same stress response as overwhelming the first time they leapt out of a plane.

This seemingly paradoxical relationship holds true for other high-performers such as athletes, surgeons, artists, actors, and musicians. A higher stress response does not predict failure; it is intimately connected to skill and mastery.

So, the key is not to avoid stressors or your stress response, and it's not to become an endlessly chilled-out and calm person.

The key to developing your resilience alongside your skills is to learn how to reframe your natural responses to stressors and welcome the stimulation, focus, and preparedness they provide.

item.title: 4 Ways Parents Can Support Teen Online Safety and Well-Being
item.description:
Adolescence

4 Ways Parents Can Support Teen Online Safety and Well-Being

A compassionate, collaborative approach can help teens navigate technology.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Strong, trusting relationships with parents do more for teens’ online safety than parental control apps.
  • Low-pressure talks about teens' online lives help them trust you enough to come to you when they need support.
  • Modeling healthy online habits is a powerful way to teach well-being and strengthen your bond with your teen.
Source: kaboompics / Pexels

I recently asked 30 young people what they wished their parents understood about their online lives. One young person’s story shows how easily parents can overlook online risks.

Blake (not their real name) was in fifth grade when an adult approached them on Amino, a now-defunct social media platform. Their conversation quickly evolved into what Blake thought of as a romantic relationship.

Looking back, Blake told me, “It was obviously incredibly unsafe,” and added, “I wish someone had found out about it earlier on.”

Blake never told their parents because they believed that they were “doing something wrong.” While Blake’s parents monitored their YouTube watch history, Blake now wishes their parents had engaged in more open conversations about their online life and set “more (tech) restrictions early on.” Contrary to what many parents might think, Blake didn’t want to be left alone. They wanted their parents to ask them about their online life and set clearer boundaries, making it easier to ask for help.

In my conversations, young people shared four practical tips for talking with teens about their online lives and supporting their online safety and well-being.

1. Be your teens’ coach, not their police officer

Due to fear of punishment or disapproval, young people often hide their online lives from parents. This secrecy is driven by the same reason teens don’t share that they were offered a drink at a party. They’re afraid it will get them in trouble, or they'll be cut off from their friends.

One young LGBTQ+ woman, for example, said that her very religious dad monitored her social media feeds and told her to delete any post he disagreed with. He did the same to her adult siblings. This didn’t stop her from posting. Instead, she learned how to moderate what he could see.

Other young people described what happened when parents responded with curiosity rather than judgment. When one young woman’s mom found her secret Twitter account, she expected to be grounded “for a million years.” Instead, her mom calmly asked who she was talking to. The young woman said that her mom’s response made room for conversation and connection.

When teens feel like they have to hide their online lives, they’re less likely to come to their parents when something goes wrong. Young people told us that when parents act as digital coaches, staying calm and walking them through difficult situations, they build online safety skills, and their relationships with their parents grow stronger. Being a coach doesn’t mean ignoring risks or abandoning rules. It means listening, understanding what happened, and helping your teen work through difficult situations.

2. Talk with teens about their online lives, even when it feels awkward

Existing research and our conversations with young people both point to the importance of talking with teens about their online lives. Similar to talking to teens about other sensitive topics like drinking and sex, it’s more effective to have the conversation before it's relevant. Think of it less like a “Sit down; we have to talk” lecture and more like a series of low-pressure chats.

There are many good conversation guides for parents, including from Internet Matters, Common Sense Media, and the Spark and Stitch Institute. By using nonjudgmental, open-ended questions such as “What’s something you’ve enjoyed online lately?” or “How do you feel about your school’s AI policy?” parents can show curiosity without making teens defensive. Current events, like the recent Meta settlement, can also serve as a springboard for conversation.

It can help to keep expectations for these conversations low. Even the best-timed and well-intentioned conversations are likely to be met with eye rolls by teens. That’s OK. As teen psychologist and author Lisa Damour explains, “Your (kid) may roll her eyes, but do it anyway. (Kids) can listen and roll their eyes at the same time.” Her podcast episode, “Untangling All Things Digital for Parents,” is worth a listen.

3. Create family tech agreements that reflect shared values

As a parent, I was surprised and heartened to learn that not all tech rules feel restrictive to teens. Several were even grateful for them. One teen boy I spoke with said, “[My parents] make me leave my phone downstairs … I think that's a good idea because I don't wanna be using my phone. I'm trying to sleep because I have to wake up really early.”

This aligns with recent research showing that teens and young adults value solo downtime, face-to-face time with friends, and sleep even more than they value time spent online. Parents can respect their teens’ desire for independence by inviting them to help draft family “tech agreements” based on shared values such as sleep, time with friends, and privacy. Internet Matters offers a family tech agreement template that works well for tweens and younger teens, and Screenagers provides broader, more flexible guidance. Use these templates as starting points and revisit the agreement as your teen’s needs and independence change.

4. What you do is more important than what you say

Young people told us that their parents’ tech use shaped their own, for better and worse. One young adult said a lack of healthy boundaries at home left “no real role model to follow.” Another said her mother now tells her to ask an AI chatbot before coming to her for advice.

Modeling healthy habits is one of the most powerful tools parents have. When parents spend a lot of time on digital media, their teens tend to do so as well. Moreover, teens who feel like their parents are more focused on their devices than on them report higher depression. Parents can strengthen their relationship and teach healthy tech habits at the same time by holding themselves to the same standards that they set for their teen. This might look like modeling the importance of sleep by agreeing that everyone in the house, including parents, keeps phones out of the bedroom after 10 p.m.

You don’t need to model perfection. You can acknowledge when you get distracted or struggle to maintain a boundary. Saying, “I’ve been checking my phone too much during dinner, so I’m going to leave it in the other room,” makes your own effort visible. Shared expectations show that healthy tech habits are a family responsibility, not just something parents impose on teens.

Parenting in the age of Big Tech is hard; go easy on yourself

Parents are being asked to make high-stakes decisions about fast-changing technology, often without shared norms or practical support. They shouldn’t have to carry this burden alone, but tech companies and federal regulatory agencies aren’t adequately stepping up.

Fortunately, you don’t need to be a tech expert to listen to teens, set thoughtful boundaries, and make it easier for your teen to ask for help. What helps teens most is a strong, trusting relationship with their parents. Research backs this up: A warm parent-child relationship, alongside clear boundaries, predicts safer internet use among teens. Over time, a compassionate and collaborative approach can help teens navigate technology skillfully, with less secrecy and power struggles and more mutual respect.
