item.title: Can Buying Your Childhood Home Bring Back the Past?
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Can Buying Your Childhood Home Bring Back the Past?

The pull of our childhood homes, and what it means to return.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Childhood homes can remain emotionally important long after we leave them.
  • Reclaiming a childhood home may bring comfort without erasing grief and loss.
  • Childhood memories and attachments can shape major decisions decades later.
  • Recovering a childhood home does not necessarily restore the life once lived there.

Think of the home where you spent your childhood. You may still remember the room you slept in, the conversations you had there, the sound of someone calling you for dinner or the family and friends who came to visit on special occasions. Even years after leaving, that house may remain closely connected to your memories and sense of self.

Some people go beyond remembering their childhood homes and decide to buy them. But can recovering a childhood home also bring back the life once lived there?

Below, I explore that question through the experiences of three people who did exactly that. What made them want to reclaim these properties, and what did they discover when they returned? Their stories invite us to consider what it means to return to a place that remains so much a part of who we are.

The childhood home he waited 12 years to buy

Eddie Dilleen is one of Australia’s largest residential landlords; he owns more than 200 properties. But there was one property he could not buy. For more than 12 years, he waited for his childhood home to go on the market.

As he has written, ‘You can set reminders and stuff like that, but when I was on my phone messing around, I would randomly check it literally every one or two weeks for the past 12 years.’ When the house finally came on the market, he said, ‘I just bought it sight unseen.’ The price was just under $1 million. The house had been sold 25 years earlier for $97,000 following his parents’ divorce.

Eddie’s childhood home remained important to him throughout his adult life, even after he achieved financial success. His constant checking on it suggests an enduring emotional attachment to a place associated with loss and family separation. His decision to purchase the house without viewing it indicates a desperation to reclaim something he felt he had lost.

His experience also may be understood in the context of cognitive immobility, which can occur when an individual is unable to stay put in an intended place due to the absence or presence of certain restrictions or circumstances beyond their control, which may originate in their present or desired location, inside themselves, or in the external world.

Circumstances beyond Dilleen’s control made him leave his childhood home but some part of him remained in it.

The childhood home she lost

Jenaca Rogers lived with her grandma but was also raised from infancy by her family friends, Pat and Jerry. Their house held many of her childhood memories, from family celebrations to everyday moments spent with her grandparents. When Pat and Jerry died, the house was sold following probate proceedings. As Jenaca recalled, ‘We were all heartbroken. Your whole life you hope for something and then it’s just taken away’.

Years later, in 2025, Jenaca unexpectedly discovered that the house was for sale, and called the estate agent. When he failed to answer, she said, ‘I just started crying because I was like, I’m not going to get it’.

She then found the agent’s mobile number online. She recalls, ‘I called him and he got us out there, and I cried in the driveway, I cried touring the house’. During the visit, she discovered her toy car in the backyard shed, which overwhelmed her further. She eventually bought the house and surprised her grandma, Connie, with a viewing. It was a homecoming for them both.

Buying the house brought Jenaca peace and comfort, but it did not erase her grief. Her experience suggests that reclaiming a meaningful place may help us feel emotionally connected with loved ones who have died but does not necessarily help with the loss.

He bought his childhood home, but not his childhood

Moving from Bogotá to Miami brought Colombian singer-songwriter Andrés Cepeda new opportunities and challenges, but he left behind something deeply personal. After years of searching for something he felt he had lost in Bogotá, he was able to recover it. Cepeda bought his childhood home.

After returning to the house, Cepeda said, 'I returned to the house, the street, the garden. Everything was just as I remembered. And yet nothing was the same. My parents were gone. My childhood was gone. Time itself had left.'

Cepeda may have experienced a sense of metaphorical homelessness, the idea that those who experience cognitive immobility may find out after returning home that ‘…no home is truly a home; even the previous home – the ancestral home – has lost its distinguishing features and allure’. Although Cepeda had recovered the property, his childhood experiences could not be recreated: 'I went on a personal tour of my life. The parks, the schools, the cafés, the houses of my friends, the places where my heart broke. All of it started turning into music.'

He wrote the song ‘Bogotá’ to express his feelings about his childhood city and family. As he describes it, ‘It captures the eerie, bittersweet feeling of returning to a place that once defined you – only to realise you miss not the place, but the person you were there’. Cepeda recovered his childhood home but could not recover his childhood. However, he could use his music to acknowledge what cannot be recovered.

Of the three stages of cognitive immobility, his music could have helped him enter the third stage, stabilisation, in which people ‘...tend to aim to retain values and pursue goals to help them with the loss, alleviating the sense of entrapment’.

An enduring love for the homes we lost

Our childhood home can remain important long after we have left it. It is a reminder of the people we knew, our relationships and the experiences we had. If your childhood home has been lost through the breakup of your family, bereavement or some other circumstance beyond your control, recovering it may become a deeply personal goal.

The experiences of Dilleen, Rogers and Cepeda show that buying a childhood home can be a chance to reconnect with a familiar place, but it does not mean returning to the life once lived there. The building may remain but the people in it, the relationships, the life that existed there will have changed. We can return to a place without recovering the past and move forward without leaving its memories behind.

item.title: How to Motivate Children for Success in School
item.description:
Education

How to Motivate Children for Success in School

8 ways to support your child's interest in learning.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Children's instinctive curiosity is the starting point for their motivation and enjoyment of learning.
  • Make note of every improvement, not every mistake.
  • Making a contribution to their communities offers children a better goal and standard for success.

Parents in America and around the world agree on this: We want our children to succeed in school. Intense pressure for academic achievement now dominates the lives of many American families.

American students, however, are not doing well. Perhaps even more concerning, they seem to have less interest in learning. High school and college teachers across the country now assign less reading to their students, and students still complain that this is more than they can manage. Many American high school and college students no longer read books!

There are several possible causes for our children's loss of interest in learning, and different causes for different children. The impact of screens is certainly important. Children no longer have the attention span for reading. Instead, they are scrolling and watching short videos. They may even believe that, in this way, they are learning.

What Can We Do?

1. Express enthusiastic interest in your child’s interests, even if these are not the interests you would choose. Learning begins with interest. Children's instinctive interest and curiosity about the world are the starting point for their motivation and enjoyment of learning. As soon as children begin to talk, they are constantly asking questions, seeking information, and wanting to know “why.” Too often, in our understandable effort to help improve their skills, we neglect this essential aspect of children’s motivation.

Make note of moments of interest and talk with your children about what interests them. Ask questions. Do "research" together. Help them develop their interests into projects and goals.

The promise of rewards or the threat of punishment may lead to some short-term improvement in a child’s effort. But rewards and punishments cannot create interest, enjoyment, or long-term goals

2. Find the source of their anxiety, frustration, and discouragement. Parents often ask, "Why doesn’t he put more effort into his schoolwork? Why doesn’t he care?” The answer to these questions is almost always, “Because he is discouraged.”

Children may mask their discouragement with defiant or rebellious attitudes, and they may pretend that they don’t care. But they do care. If we look hard enough, we will find in every child some interest and a desire to do well.

Undiagnosed attention and learning disorders are a common source of discouragement and lack of sustained effort in children and adolescents. It is essential for parents and teachers to understand the impact of these difficulties. Even mild or moderate learning problems can be a source of anxiety, frustration, and low self-esteem.

3. Make note of every improvement, not every mistake. To solve the problem of discouragement, children need more encouragement and less criticism. Of course, to improve their skills, children need criticism. But they need encouragement even more. Encouragement is not false praise. We all need encouragement, even as adults, with every new challenge and skill we attempt to master.

4. Help them cultivate a growth mindset. Praise effort, not intelligence or talent. Praise learning, not grades. Then, on this foundation, we can set high standards and challenge children to work harder. But we will have to do this less often, because they will more often challenge themselves.

5. Appreciate their strengths. Students who seem unmotivated are often focused on their weaknesses, not on their strengths.

When I talk with “unmotivated” children, I often find qualities of intelligence, creativity, effort, and character that their parents and teachers have overlooked and that they may also fail to appreciate. When I point out these qualities, many children and adolescents feel deeply understood. For some, this is a transformative moment. Years later, these affirming statements are what they remember and value most about our work.

6. Make learning meaningful. Individual achievement alone—getting good grades in school—is a fragile source of motivation and effort, with a high cost in anxiety and stress. If we define achievement, however, as making a contribution to our families, our communities, our country, and the world, we offer children a much better goal and standard for success. We should help them become involved in projects that help their community, and we should be involved with them.

7. Have conversations. Every moment of dialogue with our children and grandchildren adds meaning and relevance to learning. Talk with your children about what they are studying—about civics and history, science, literature, and religion—and the importance of these subjects to our current lives. Talk with them about how others help us, about the good work that many people are doing, and what they can do to help others.

Conversation is a (partial) antidote to the addictive pull of screens. Before you ask, “Have you done your homework?” ask them about what they have been learning in school.

8. Establish "library hours" in your home. Even when children are highly motivated to do well in school, they still need to establish good work habits. They need to put away their devices, do their homework, and get enough sleep.

I encourage parents to set aside a specified time, early in the evening, as a homework or “library” hour. During the library hour, all electronics should be turned off (except for computers or tablets children need for schoolwork) for the entire family. No television, no video games, no phones.

Homework should be done in a communal place (as in a library), at the kitchen or dining room table. Especially with younger children, parents are present and available to help, offer encouragement, and answer questions. Then, when homework is done, there is time for play.

Most families have found these guidelines helpful for students of all ages. The result is an important lesson in self-discipline, fewer family arguments, and more success in school.

item.title: Childhood Trauma and Grief: Lessons From Batman and Two-Face
item.description:
Adverse Childhood Experiences

Childhood Trauma and Grief: Lessons From Batman and Two-Face

Why the same early losses can fragment one person and forge another.

Posted November 17, 2026

Key points
  • Childhood adversity creates living losses: grief that is re-experienced across a lifetime.
  • Traumatic loss and grief that goes unexpressed can leave the psyche surviving in pieces, as Two-Face shows.
  • A secure relationship, like Alfred’s with Bruce Wayne, helps turn grief into something that can be integrated.
Source: Sajjad Ahmadi / Unsplash

The difference between a heroic caped crusader and a criminal mastermind may come down to who was waiting in the doorway after a very bad childhood.

Harvey Dent (Two-Face) and Bruce Wayne (Batman) both carry the weight of living losses: grief from a traumatic childhood that never fully ends. Bruce becomes Gotham’s protector, while Harvey becomes Two-Face, a sadistic supervillain who mirrors the abuse he internalized as a child. Their stories show how loss is shaped by the context in which it occurs.

We usually think of grief as something that follows a death, but some of the deepest grief comes from what never was, such as a safe, loving, and reliable family. Grief researchers call this nonfinite loss, or living loss. It is re-experienced throughout life and keeps demanding adjustment.1

The losses no one sees

In "The Dark Knight," Harvey is a driven, idealistic district attorney who becomes Two-Face after violence takes the woman he loves.2 The comics reveal an earlier story: a father who abused him, with outcomes decided by the flip of a coin.3,4 Long before that night, Harvey had lost security, trust, innocence, and a sense of his own authenticity. These are intangible losses, which are symbolic, invisible, more existential, and easy to bury under professional achievements.

His story is also less rare and outlandish than it seems. The World Health Organization estimates that about six in ten adults in North America and four in ten in Europe have had at least one adverse childhood experience (ACE).5 ACEs are correlated with increased risks of being involved in the criminal justice system, health-harming behaviours, poor psychological health, and poverty or homelessness, and higher mortality rates, in addition to chronic illnesses.

When the psyche splits

Early relationships teach us how to regulate ourselves and what to expect from the world.6 When caregivers become a source of threat, a child adapts. Parts of our psyche hide, go numb, or freeze. Freeze is a psychobiological conservation strategy that results in having fractured developmental egoic states; we adapt by hiding, repressing, or emotionally isolating certain aspects of ourselves, analogous to how we have been made to feel by others.7

Jungian analyst Donald Kalsched describes how a traumatized psyche will survive in pieces when it is not safe to be whole.8 Two-Face is what happens when that adaptation becomes literal and hardens into identity: a polarized psyche, split between idealism and rage. He demonstrates how unexpressed grief does not disappear, and how traumatic loss can tear us apart from the inside.

Why Bruce didn’t become a villain

Bruce has his own devastating losses.9 The difference is Alfred, a secure attachment figure who is consistent, attuned, and present when it matters. With Alfred, Bruce could grieve beside someone instead of alone, and being able to access the right support allowed Bruce to engage in his grief in a more integrative way than Harvey.

While Bruce nonetheless demonstrates his own childhood attachment injury from the death of his parents, his relationship with his parents is portrayed as positive in the Batman films and comics. This highlights how Bruce had internalized what it means to be protected, co-regulated with when distressed, and supported by loving attachment figures in expressing his own autonomy or interdependence at a young age.

This illuminates how loss experiences are always shaped by the various relational contexts in which they occur. In practice, that means finding our own Alfred, as we all need a trusted and caring person who can help us tend old losses. It also means cultivating an inner Alfred within our own imagination—a steady, compassionate aspect of ourselves that helps us stay grounded when the pain surfaces, even when it is not possible to find such a person externally to us.

This piece draws on my book chapter, Shadows in Context: Two-Face, Batman, and Losses Associated with a Traumatic Childhood in Superhero Grief and the Multiverse of Loss: Considerations and Case Studies edited by Jill Harrington and Darcy Harris (2026), which is a new collection published by Routledge that uses superheroes and the multiverse to explore the impact of non-death loss on our psychology.10
